clinicalPearls: A congenital disorder of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor biosynthesis, most often from PIGV mutations, with other PIG/PGAP genes implicated
Cardinal features are persistently raised serum alkaline phosphatase (hyperphosphatasia), intellectual disability, and seizures
The paradoxical hyperphosphatasia arises because alkaline phosphatase, a GPI-anchored enzyme, is shed into the circulation when its anchor is defective
Additional features include distinctive facial dysmorphism, brachytelephalangy (short distal phalanges with hypoplastic nails), and variable neurological impairment
Some patients have Hirschsprung disease, anorectal or other structural anomalies as part of the phenotypic spectrum
The persistently elevated alkaline phosphatase is the biochemical clue that prompts consideration of a GPI-anchor defect rather than bone or liver disease
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, targeting seizures, developmental support, and associated anomalies, as no specific corrective therapy exists
reference.pathophysiology: The GPI anchor tethers numerous proteins to the outer cell membrane. PIGV and related genes encode enzymes in the GPI biosynthetic pathway; loss-of-function mutations impair anchor assembly, so GPI-anchored proteins are either misprocessed or released rather than retained at the cell surface. Alkaline phosphatase is a GPI-anchored ectoenzyme, so a defective anchor causes it to be secreted into plasma, producing the characteristic hyperphosphatasia. Disruption of other GPI-anchored proteins essential for neuronal function underlies the intellectual disability and seizures, while developmental roles of affected proteins explain the dysmorphism, digital anomalies, and structural malformations. The disorder therefore links a striking laboratory finding to a neurodevelopmental syndrome through a shared membrane-anchoring defect.
additionalDifferentials: Metabolic or hepatic causes of raised alkaline phosphatase
Other syndromic intellectual disability with seizures
Skeletal dysplasia with elevated alkaline phosphatase
additionalInvestigations: Serum alkaline phosphatase, persistently and unexplainedly elevated
Flow cytometry for GPI-anchored surface proteins on blood cells where available
Developmental and neurological assessment with EEG for seizures
Evaluation for Hirschsprung disease and anorectal or other structural anomalies when suggested
Molecular testing of PIGV and other GPI-anchor pathway genes
redFlags: Feeding difficulty or bowel obstruction suggesting Hirschsprung disease
Structural cardiac or renal anomalies requiring intervention
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is determined by the severity of neurological impairment and associated malformations; many affected individuals have lifelong intellectual disability and epilepsy, and management remains supportive since no disease-modifying therapy is established.
pitfalls: Chasing bone or liver disease to explain the raised alkaline phosphatase and missing the GPI-anchor defect
Overlooking the diagnostic significance of persistent hyperphosphatasia in a child with developmental delay and seizures
Missing associated Hirschsprung disease or anorectal anomalies
Assuming the elevated alkaline phosphatase reflects increased bone turnover requiring treatment
references: Nyhan's Atlas of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
management: Anticonvulsant therapy for seizures, with a trial of pyridoxine given reported responsiveness in some GPI-anchor defects
Early developmental intervention, special educational support and physiotherapy for intellectual disability and neurological impairment
Surgical management of Hirschsprung disease and anorectal or other structural anomalies where present
Assessment and management of associated malformations including brain imaging and evaluation of the digital and skeletal features
Multidisciplinary care coordinated across paediatric neurology, clinical genetics, surgery and developmental services
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with family screening
